chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Abu Ja'far, from his father, from Wahb, from Ja'far, from his father, that Ali (peace be upon him) said:
The mudabbarr (slave manumitted upon payment of a fixed sum) is not sold except from his own self.

This report carries two meanings: one is that he is not sold on behalf of others, but rather it is preferable that he be sold from his own self, just as the mukatab is sold in the same manner; if he desires that, then that is considered recommended, because the earlier reports are general regarding the permissibility of selling him to whomever one wishes.

The other meaning is that only the self of the mudabbarr is sold, and his children are not sold; and when he returns in his manumission (by paying the rest of the price), his children do not return in their manumission, according to what was detailed earlier in the narration of Aban ibn Ghutfan.
And the mudabbarr and his children are counted from the third (of the estate for bequests); if their price exceeds one-third, they are asked to pay the remainder for the heir.

key_terms.الْمُدَبَّرُ: A slave manumitted upon payment of a fixed sum
key_terms.الْمُكَاتَبُ: A slave contracted to pay a sum for manumission

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a mudabbarr and his children in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Isfabar highlights the juristic debate regarding the sale of a *mudabbarr* (slave contracted for manumission), distinguishing between selling the slave's debt obligation versus the slave's personhood. It clarifies that while the *mudabbarr* and his children are treated as a single unit for inheritance calculations, their manumission price is deducted from the estate's one-third bequest limit, with any excess borne by the heir. This reflects the Shia emphasis on the financial autonomy of the *mudabbarr* and the specific rules governing the liquidation of their freedom within the broader framework of Islamic inheritance law.
